fatal_errors: It does not identify annealing-temperature control followed by water quenching as the specific method used to control phase evolution.
It incorrectly emphasizes compositional variation, although the target study held the Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 composition fixed and varied annealing temperature.
It omits the cooling-induced spinodal decomposition, reciprocal BCC/B2 partitioning, and subsequent Ni–Al ordering that explain why the method works.
It provides none of the relevant 1100–1300 °C annealing conditions, phase-fraction trends, or hardness results.
explanation: The hypothesis is broadly aligned with the idea that processing can influence phases in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, but it is too generic to reconstruct the target. The relevant control method is high-temperature annealing under argon at selected temperatures followed by rapid water quenching. Changing the annealing temperature changes the high-temperature BCC/FCC stability, while cooling drives spinodal separation of BCC into Ni–Al-lean and Ni–Al-rich products and ordering of the latter into B2. These transformations produce reciprocal hierarchical BCC/B2 structures and increasing hardness with higher quench temperature. The proposed systematic experiment using XRD and microscopy is directionally sensible, but lacks fixed composition, specified temperatures, quenching, hardness measurements, B2-sensitive diffraction/TEM, and compositional mapping needed to discriminate the target mechanism.
